goals.motivation: More creative work while preserving stability
goals.description: Move into independent digital design work near my current home

chapter.body:
In November, you begin making room for design after the administration workday ends. Some evenings become practice evenings—not a departure from your current life, but a deliberate adjustment within it. Digital design exercises ask for the hours that work has left untouched. You have eight hours a week available, and making use of them takes planning rather than a sudden burst of freedom.

The pace is manageable. You build digital design fundamentals while keeping your job, letting the two sit alongside each other. There is reassurance in that arrangement: your monthly income remains 400,000 HUF, and your liquid funds remain 1,200,000 HUF. You want more creative work, but you want the stability to stay. Independent design near your current home in Veszprém is the direction—not a move abroad, not a leap that requires everything familiar to disappear.

By January, visual layout has joined your growing set of skills. Then a local business posts a limited website-refresh brief. The word “limited” makes it tempting. Here is something more concrete than an exercise: a possible first practical project, close enough to fit the life you are trying to build.

You pause over the brief. Taking it on could give your practice a different purpose, but the evenings are already doing a job. They are where you study, and they also leave some space to recover. A project would not create more time simply because it mattered to you.

In March, you review the fit again. Your administration job is still there; your design practice is still there. You measure the possible commitment against the same eight available hours. Nothing has been accepted. Looking carefully is not the same as saying yes, and for now the distinction lets you examine the opportunity without making it an obligation.

Then April 3 arrives: the deadline. The brief remains open, but you can no longer leave the question comfortably in the distance.

Accepting would mean keeping your current job while making room for a first client experience, with only four hours a week left available. Declining would protect your study time while closing this particular opening. Letting the deadline pass would preserve your routine and leave the broader local-design goal intact, though this project would be gone.

You return to the brief with those three possibilities in view. Which matters most for what you build next: trying your skills on a limited project, protecting the time to develop them, or letting this opening pass while keeping the larger path open?
chapter.title: Room for Something of Your Own

chapter.body:
In May, you approach the accepted website-refresh brief one manageable step at a time. The work must fit around your administration job, not replace it. Four hours a week gives you room to begin, but not much room to lose your way.

You study the requests, then return to the part you can address next. The glow of the design work offers a different kind of attention from the office day: spacing, emphasis, the relationship between words and layout. You want more of this creative work, close to your current home in Veszprém. For now, wanting it means keeping the scope small enough to hold alongside the stability you also value.

By June, the brief is teaching you something beyond visual layout. A client's request can contain several tasks folded into one sentence. You practice separating them, putting them in order, deciding what belongs within this limited piece of work. Your existing planning and writing skills help, but shaping a client brief becomes a skill of its own.

There is satisfaction in making the work clearer before trying to make it better. You do not have to solve everything at once. You need a sequence you can follow when an evening contains only a little time and attention.

In August, you take stock. Your administration job remains in place; your monthly income is still 400,000 HUF, and your liquid funds remain 1,200,000 HUF. The brief has not turned into a new career by itself. What it has given you is practical experience to consider alongside the design fundamentals you already had.

You still want independent digital design work near home. Evening practice remains an acceptable tradeoff, but the hours cannot be considered separately from the energy they ask of you. You weigh the project, the office work, and the space left between them. Is the current rhythm something to preserve, something to stretch, or something to ease?

By October, that question is ready for a decision. Each path leaves you employed and in Hungary. Keeping four hours a week would preserve your present balance; progress may be gradual, with room for consistency. Setting aside six hours could create more momentum, but would tighten your schedule and leave less energy for other things. Reducing the commitment to two hours would protect more recovery time; the transition may feel slower, though the pace could be more comfortable.

You have a practical starting point, not a settled answer. How much time and energy do you want to give independent design work over the next stretch?
chapter.title: Room for the Work

events.title: Turning project experience into a clearer direction
events.summary: You look back on what you learned from the local website-refresh brief and the design skills you have been building. It gives you a more concrete sense of the kind of independent work you might pursue, without making the next step obvious.

events.title: Making space to assess the workload
events.summary: You take stock of design practice alongside your administration job. The current pace has kept the goal in view, but you are weighing whether to protect more time and energy or make a stronger push toward building independent work.

events.title: Choosing your next six-month rhythm
events.summary: Your experience so far offers a starting point, not a guarantee of where independent design work will lead. You can keep the present pace, ease back to protect energy, or make a more demanding commitment while staying employed and near home.

decision.prompt: How would you like to balance design-work progress with time and energy over the next six months?

options.label: Protect more room to recover
options.description: Reduce the weekly hours you set aside for design and give yourself more energy margin. This may make progress slower, but could leave more capacity for your job and everyday life.

options.label: Keep the current steady pace
options.description: Continue setting aside the same amount of time and energy. This preserves momentum without adding a new workload, though progress may remain gradual.

options.label: Make a more demanding push
options.description: Set aside more weekly time for design practice and building toward independent work. This could create room for faster progress, but leaves less energy for other parts of your routine.

chapter.body:
On November 19, you return in thought to the local website-refresh brief. What stays with you is not a grand turning point, but a clearer outline: the space between what someone asks for and what a design needs to do. Your planning and writing skills belong in that space, alongside visual layout, digital design fundamentals, and the work of scoping a brief.

Independent design no longer feels quite so abstract. You can picture the kind of work you might pursue near your current home in Veszprém, without imagining an entirely different life around it. That distinction matters. You want more creative work, but you also want the stability your administration job provides. One wish does not cancel the other.

There is still no obvious next step. Looking back gives you something to work from, not a guarantee.

By February 8, the question has shifted from what interests you to how much room you can give it. Six hours a week sounds modest until you set it beside your job and the energy needed for ordinary life. Evening study is a tradeoff you are willing to make; willingness, though, does not make an evening longer.

You pause over that tension. Protecting time for design keeps the goal visible. Protecting energy keeps the pursuit from taking up every available corner. Neither feels like a trivial concern.

Your circumstances remain steady: you are still employed in administration, with a monthly income of HUF 400,000 and HUF 1,200,000 in liquid funds. Those figures are part of the stability you want to preserve, not evidence that independent work is ready to replace it. You have experience to reflect on and skills to practise, but no certainty to borrow from the future.

On April 3, the horizon narrows to a more manageable question: the next six months. You do not have to decide your entire working life today. You do have to consider the rhythm that could carry this goal alongside the life you already have.

Four hours a week would leave more room to recover, accepting that progress might be slower. Six would preserve the present pace, with its familiar balance and gradual momentum. Eight would make a stronger commitment to design practice and building toward independence, while leaving less energy elsewhere. In each version, you would remain employed and near home.

The choice is not between caring about the goal and abandoning it. It is between different ways of making room for something you care about. How much time—and how much of yourself—do you want to give it over the next six months?
